input: This case sets out the inventory policy for a spare motor. Based on the analysis that has been carried out, the safety stock for the spare motor is set at 1991 units, a level that corresponds to a 95% cycle service level. The policy is built on the following demand picture: mean demand runs at 3878 units per week, with a standard deviation of 456 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 7 weeks. Over a lead time of that length, the expected demand comes to 3878 × 7 = 27146 units, so the reorder point, which combines the lead-time demand with the safety stock, works out at 27146 + 1991 = 29137 units. When the stock position falls to that level, a replenishment order should be placed. The 95% cycle service level represents the balance that has been struck between holding stock on the shelf and accepting the risk of running out during a replenishment cycle. The policy is deliberately simple to operate: the figures it needs are the demand history summarised in the mean and the standard deviation, together with the lead time quoted for replenishment, and no other inputs are required. It is important to note the assumptions on which the policy rests: demand is treated as normally distributed and as independent from one week to the next, and seasonal peaks are excluded from the analysis altogether. This means that the policy, while robust within its stated basis, does not make any provision for seasonal peaks, and it would need to be revisited if the demand pattern, the lead time or the variability of demand were to change materially.
target: Safety stock for the spare motor is 1991 units, held by inventory control at a 95% cycle service level. The policy rests on mean demand of 3878 units per week, a standard deviation of 456 units per week and a replenishment lead time of 7 weeks. Demand over the lead time is 3878 × 7 = 27146 units. The reorder point is the lead-time demand plus the safety stock, 27146 + 1991 = 29137 units; a replenishment order is placed when the stock position reaches the reorder point. The 95% cycle service level is the point the policy sets on the trade-off between stock held and cycles in which demand exhausts the shelf before replenishment arrives. The two components of the reorder point do different work. The lead-time demand covers the expected consumption while a replenishment order is in transit, and it is set by the mean alone. The safety stock covers the variability around that mean, and it is set by the standard deviation together with the service level the policy chooses. A change in variability therefore moves the safety stock without moving the lead-time demand, and a change in the mean moves both. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks, and the safety stock is computed on that basis. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the policy basis, and the safety stock makes no provision for them. The stock position against which the reorder point is tested is the position the stores ledger reports for the motor, and the comparison is made on that reported figure. Inventory control recomputes the safety stock when the mean demand, the lead time or the demand variability changes, because each of the three enters the figure directly.
